#### Last Updated: `r Sys.Date()`

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(HyperCom)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges)
library(Matrix)
library(tidyr)
```

## Inputs
HyperCom requires three inputs. Most failed runs come from one of these points, so check them first:

1. **Counts:** a gene x cell matrix with genes as row names and cells as column names, sparse or dense. Raw or normalised counts
   give the same results, since HyperCom only uses whether each gene is above 0 in each cell; never use scaled data (negative
   values stop the run). Cell names must be unique across samples: prefix the barcodes with their sample when merging samples.

2. **Cell metadata:** a dataframe with one row per cell, its row names being the cell names of the counts, with a sample column
   and optionally a group column. The sample is the library or replicate: cells are only compared with cells of their own sample,
   so every sample needs at least 2 cells that express a ligand or receptor gene. The group is the condition, for priorities
   specific to a group. Cells of the counts without a row in the metadata are left out, with a warning.

3. **Ligand-receptor (LR) interactions** whose gene symbols match the species of the counts. HyperCom contains 2 built in LR
   databases formatted properly:

    + CellChat human `cellchat.hs.lrdb` (gene symbols such as `TGFB1`)

    + CellChat mouse `cellchat.mm.lrdb` (gene symbols such as `Tgfb1`)

In this vignette we will use a 1000 cell subset of heart failure from [Alexanian et al, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03674-1).
This example subset is included in the package as `alexanian2021.counts` and `alexanian2021.metadata`; its counts are
log-normalised.
```{r}
counts <- alexanian2021.counts
dim(counts)
head(rownames(counts))
head(colnames(counts))
```

```{r}
cell.meta <- alexanian2021.metadata
head(cell.meta)
table(cell.meta$sample, cell.meta$condition)
```

```{r}
ggplot(cell.meta, aes(x=UMAP_1, y=UMAP_2, colour=celltype)) +
  geom_point(size=0.5) +
  theme_classic()
```

For the LR interactions we will use the CellChat murine database. The first column names the interaction, the second is the
ligand and the others the receptor genes (NA where a receptor complex has fewer subunits).
```{r}
lrdb <- cellchat.mm.lrdb
dim(lrdb)
```

```{r}
head(lrdb, 2)
```

## Running HyperCom
The whole pipeline runs with one call to `HyperCom`. It writes every step to `outdir` and returns the results as a list, so they
need not be read back. `parallel=TRUE` uses one thread per physical core and `threads` sets the number directly (the default is
one thread). `significance=TRUE` adds p-values and `seed` makes them reproducible.
```{r}
outdir <- file.path(tempdir(), "overview")
res <- HyperCom(lrdb=cellchat.mm.lrdb, counts=alexanian2021.counts,
                metadata=alexanian2021.metadata, sample="sample",
                group="condition", significance=TRUE, seed=1,
                parallel=TRUE, outdir=outdir, verbose=FALSE)
head(res$priority[["1"]])
```

The files are numbered in the order of the steps below: `0.counts.rds` (the filtered counts), `1.lrs.csv` (the interactions
whose genes are all expressed), `2.hyperedges.csv`, `3.adj.rds` (the adjacency matrix), `4.infMat.rds` (the influence matrix),
`5.metadata.csv` and one `6.priority/priority.<weight>.csv` per weight. CSV files read back with `read.csv`; the `.rds` files with
`readRDS` after `library(HyperCom)`.
```{r}
list.files(outdir, recursive=TRUE)
priority <- read.csv(file.path(outdir, "6.priority", "priority.1.csv"))
infMat <- readRDS(file.path(outdir, "4.infMat.rds"))
```

For a Seurat object, `HyperCom_seurat` reads one layer of one assay (by default the `counts` layer of the `RNA` assay, Seurat v5 or
older assays) and the cell metadata; `sample`, `group` and `keep` name columns of the cell metadata (`seurat[[]]`). It needs the
SeuratObject package.
```{r, eval=FALSE}
res <- HyperCom_seurat(seurat=seurat_object, lrdb=cellchat.mm.lrdb, sample="sample",
                       assay="RNA", layer="counts", group="condition",
                       parallel=TRUE, outdir="overview")
```

### Run time and memory
Memory grows with the number of cells per sample squared, since cells are compared within their sample: more samples of the same
size cost little. Measured with `parallel=TRUE` on a 16-core desktop; the two larger rows score a tenth of the CellChat pairs (about
100) without p-values, so all pairs take about ten times as long, and p-values add 1000 background pairs:

| cells | samples | time | memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 (this vignette) | 2 | seconds | under 1 GB |
| 20,000 | 3 | about 1.3 min | about 3.5 GB |
| 50,000 | 3 | about 10 min | about 17 GB |

The influence matrix is never built in full by default, so its memory grows with the number of cells rather than its square.
`infmat.method="lu"` builds it in full and reproduces the numbers of HyperCom 0.0.0.9000 exactly (the default agrees with them to
about 1e-15), at the cost of two matrices of all cells and genes squared.

### Runs that stop
Scoring the pairs takes almost all of the run time, hours on large data. While pairs are scored, `HyperCom` keeps the pairs
scored so far in `<outdir>/6.priority/cache`, so a run that stops (the time limit of a cluster job, a crash, a closed R session)
loses little. Run the same call again: the steps before the scoring are repeated (seconds for 50,000 cells) and the scoring
continues from the cache, losing at most the last batch of pairs. The results are the same as those of a run that never stopped
on the same type of computer (on a cluster, ask for the same node type: another CPU can change the last digits, about 1e-13);
without `seed`, the run continues with the background pairs it drew before the stop. A continued run says so in its messages, e.g.
`Continuing from the cache in overview/6.priority/cache: 812 of 2042 pairs already scored`.

The cache folder is removed once the priority files are written. A cache made from other inputs (other counts, metadata or
`infmat.method`) is not used: it is moved to `cache.old`, with a warning, and can be renamed back to continue the run it belongs to.
If the cache cannot be written (e.g. a full disk), scoring goes on without it. `cache=FALSE` keeps no cache. `prioritize_lr` keeps it in `<outdir>/cache` the same
way, and keeps none with `outdir=NULL`.

On a cluster, a job can therefore ask for less time than the whole run and be submitted again, with the same script, until it
finishes:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
res <- HyperCom(lrdb=cellchat.mm.lrdb, counts=counts, metadata=cell.meta,
                sample="sample", group="condition", significance=TRUE, seed=1,
                parallel=TRUE, outdir="overview")
```

## Running HyperCom step by step
The rest of this vignette runs each component function of the pipeline in turn, with `outfile=NULL` so nothing is written.

### Preprocessing
In order to reduce memory usage, we first filter the counts matrix to only genes present in the LR interactions with expression greater than 0.
The function also transposes the matrix.
```{r}
lr.counts <- filter_counts(counts=counts, lrdb=lrdb, outfile=NULL)
dim(lr.counts)
```

Next we filter the ligand receptor interactions to only interactions where all genes are present in the filtered expression matrix.
```{r}
lrs <- generate_lrs_table(counts=lr.counts, lrdb=lrdb, outfile=NULL)
dim(lrs)
```

### Generating Hypergraph
To generate the hyperedges, which are edges that contain multiple nodes, we use the expression matrix and the LR interactions to create 2 types of hyperedges:

1. expression edges - edges containing a ligand or receptor gene and the cells that express it

2. interaction edges - edges containing the genes that comprise an LR interaction

HyperCom represents these hyperedges as a dataframe with an edge and node column where the node belongs to the edge. The weight is set to 1 for each edge.
```{r}
hyperedges <- generate_hyperedges(counts=lr.counts, lrs=lrs, outfile=NULL)
head(hyperedges, 2)
```

We can represent this hypergraph as an adjacency matrix where the nodes are the cells, ligand genes, and receptor genes.
Each entry is the number of hyperedges shared by nodes.
The matrix is not stored: `adj` keeps which nodes are in which hyperedge, which is much smaller, and works like a matrix
(`dim(adj)`, `adj[i, j]`, `as.matrix(adj)` for the whole matrix).
```{r}
adj <- generate_adjacency_matrix(hyperedges=hyperedges, outfile=NULL)
dim(adj)
adj[c("Thbs1", "Sdc4"), 1:3]
```

### Calculating Network Connectivity
In order to calculate the network connectivity of the hypergraph we perform a random walk with restart on the adjacency matrix to
produce an influence matrix: entry (i, j) is the share of a walk started at node i that ends at node j, so each row sums to 1. At
every step the walk returns to its start with the restart probability `r`, so about `r` of each node's influence stays on the node
itself and the rest spreads over the nodes it shares hyperedges with. `generate_infMat` takes `r` (default 0.5); `HyperCom` always
uses 0.5. On this example the ranking of LR pairs hardly depends on it: `r` = 0.1 and 0.8 give the same top 20 pairs as 0.5. Like
the adjacency matrix, the influence matrix works like a matrix without being stored in full.
```{r}
infMat <- generate_infMat(adj=adj, r=0.5, outfile=NULL)
dim(infMat)
infMat[c("Thbs1", "Sdc4"), 1:3]
```

### Preparing Metadata
To account for genes now being present in the matrices, we then process the metadata to contain information on the genes as well as cell metadata.
Additionally to reduce memory, we reduce the number of columns to just cell, sample, and group; gene nodes get `"gene"` in each.
Optionally other metadata columns can be kept with `keep`.
```{r}
node.meta <- generate_metadata(infMat=infMat, metadata=cell.meta,
                               sample="sample", group="condition",
                               keep=NULL, outfile=NULL)
head(node.meta)
```

## Downstream Analysis

### Identifying Important LR Pairs
We can also identify important LR pairs by using HyperCom scoring on LR pairs.
This prioritization scores LR pairs to find highly communicative LR pairs that are optionally group specific.
The priority of a pair is the weighted geometric mean of five terms of the cells that express its genes: their fraction of all
cells, the smallest fraction of cells expressing one of its genes, the mean of each cell's larger score as sender or receiver, how
evenly they split into senders and receivers, and how much they concentrate in some groups.
The `weights` arg sets how much the fraction of cells counts: 1 (the default) weighs it like the other terms and smaller values
favor pairs specific to fewer cells; a vector of weights gives one result each.
```{r}
priority <- prioritize_lr(lrs=lrs, adj=adj, infMat=infMat, metadata=node.meta,
                          weights=c(1, 0.5), parallel=TRUE, outdir=NULL,
                          verbose=FALSE)
head(priority[["1"]])
```

The result has one table per weight, with the columns of the LR table and the priority. With `significance=TRUE`, as in the
`HyperCom` call above, it also has p and p.adj: p is the fraction of 1000 background pairs of random genes whose priority is at
least as high, so it moves in steps of 0.001 and 0 means none was as high (background pairs that get no priority are left out, with
a warning); p.adj is its Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. This takes about four times as long.
```{r}
head(res$priority[["1"]][, c("interaction", "priority", "p", "p.adj")])
```

### Scoring Cells
We see that Thbs1-Sdc4 is the highest scoring LR pair. We can calculate HyperCom scores for this pair. Each pair of cells i and j
of a sample is scored by how strongly cell i reaches the ligand and the receptor reaches cell j, relative to how strongly i reaches
j; these scores are percent-ranked together. A cell's `sender` score is its average rank as cell i and its `receiver` score its
average rank as cell j (between 0 and 1); `dif` is receiver - sender, `avg` their mean and `max` the larger. The HyperCom score
`hypercom` is the sign of `dif` times the percent rank of its size among the cells times `avg`: negative for senders, positive for
receivers. Cells with no path to the pair's genes get NaN.
```{r}
Thbs1_Sdc4 <- score_hypercom(infMat=infMat, metadata=node.meta, ligand="Thbs1",
                             receptors="Sdc4")
head(Thbs1_Sdc4[, c("cell", "sender", "receiver", "max", "hypercom")])
```

On the UMAP, senders are blue and receivers orange; cells that express no ligand or receptor gene are not in the hypergraph and
stay grey.
```{r}
umap <- data.frame(cell=rownames(cell.meta), UMAP_1=cell.meta$UMAP_1, UMAP_2=cell.meta$UMAP_2)
umap <- left_join(umap, Thbs1_Sdc4[, c("cell", "hypercom")], by=join_by(cell))
ggplot(umap, aes(x=UMAP_1, y=UMAP_2, colour=hypercom)) +
  geom_point(size=0.5) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low="#0074a7", mid="grey90", high="#e69c25", na.value="grey70") +
  ggtitle("Thbs1-Sdc4") +
  theme_classic()
```

If we plot the sender and receiver score we see both higher densities of sender and receiver cells in TAC.
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
Thbs1_Sdc4 <- left_join(Thbs1_Sdc4, node.meta, by=join_by(cell))
melt.Thbs1_Sdc4 <- pivot_longer(dplyr::select(Thbs1_Sdc4, c(cell, group, sender, receiver)), !c(cell, group), names_to = "type", values_to = "score")

ggplot(melt.Thbs1_Sdc4, aes(x = score, y = type, fill=group)) +
    geom_density_ridges(alpha=0.4) +
    xlim(0.25, 1) +
    xlab("Score") +
    ylab("Score Type") +
    ggtitle("Thbs1-Sdc4") +
    theme_classic()
```

For a receptor complex, give all its subunits: the scores of the subunits are averaged.
```{r}
Tgfb1_Tgfbr <- score_hypercom(infMat=infMat, metadata=node.meta, ligand="Tgfb1",
                              receptors=c("Tgfbr1", "Tgfbr2"))
head(Tgfb1_Tgfbr[, c("cell", "sender", "receiver", "hypercom")])
```
